verses.note: Homage to the son is homage to God, since rebellion against one was rebellion against both (verse 2). The New Testament presents every knee bowing to the exalted Christ to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:9-11).

Peter moves from this verse to Christ exalted to the right hand of God (Acts 2:33-34), connecting the psalm's ‘right hand’ with Psalm 110:1. The one not abandoned to Sheol now sits in the place of pleasures forever.

This is the verse behind the creed's line that Christ ‘sits at the right hand’ of the Father. The seat at God's right hand is not a place but a share in God's rule, given by God and exercised until every enemy is subdued.

The psalm that began with enthronement ends with the king's head lifted up. The sequence of humble refreshment on the road and then exaltation is the pattern the New Testament sees in Christ, who humbled himself and was highly exalted (Philippians 2:8-9).

The Servant's story is told from its ending: whatever follows in the song, God's verdict is that he will be exalted. The New Testament reads the resurrection and ascension of Jesus as exactly that verdict (Philippians 2:9).

The song ends as it began (52:13), with the Servant exalted, now as a victor dividing spoil. His exaltation is the reward of his self-emptying: because he poured out his life. Paul's hymn in Philippians 2:7-9 follows the same pattern, and ‘therefore’ in 2:9 answers to ‘therefore’ here.

Because the figure travels to the Ancient of Days, some interpreters, including N. T. Wright (Jesus and the Victory of God, 1996), argue that Jesus' use of the verse speaks first of his vindication and enthronement, fulfilled in his resurrection and ascension, rather than only of a descent to earth.

The universal service given to this figure is the Old Testament background for Philippians 2:9-11, where every knee bows and every tongue confesses Jesus as Lord. The early church's worship of Christ drew on texts like this one in which God shares his kingdom and honor with a human figure at his side.
‘On earth’ anticipates the risen Christ's ‘in heaven and on earth’ (28:18). The authority he exercises in Capernaum is the authority he will hold as the exalted Son of Man.

The Messiah is David's Lord because God seats him at his right hand, sharing God's rule. The New Testament reads the verse as fulfilled in Jesus' resurrection and ascension, and the church confesses it in the creeds: he sits at the right hand of the Father.
On any reading, the verse presents Jesus as the Son of Man who receives God's kingdom and glory. The one about to be handed over and killed (14:41) will be seen in power.

Jesus combines Psalm 110 and Daniel 7 to describe his vindication after rejection. The one about to be condemned claims God's right hand, which is where the apostles proclaim him after the resurrection (Acts 2:33-36, 7:56).
Sitting at God's right hand means sharing God's rule. The crucified one now reigns, which is why the next verse can speak of the Lord working with his messengers from heaven.

Luke defines the goal of the road not only as the cross but as the taking up. The days being fulfilled point beyond Jerusalem's judgment to the ascension, so the whole travel narrative moves toward Jesus' exaltation through suffering.

The maxim describes the pattern of Christ's own story: he humbled himself to death on a cross, and God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:8-9). Luke repeats the saying after the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector (18:14), where the one who goes home justified is the one who humbled himself before God.

The kingdom is received elsewhere, not seized in Jerusalem. In Daniel 7:13-14 the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days to be given dominion, and Luke's Jesus receives his kingship in the same way, by going to the Father.

The psalm moves from rejection to exaltation by God's act. In the parable the son stays dead; the quotation adds what the story could not, that God will reverse the builders' verdict. Peter preaches this very text to the same council after the resurrection (Acts 4:10-11).

The psalm speaks of one enthroned beside God, sharing his rule while God subdues his enemies. Luke will apply it to the risen Jesus exalted to God's right hand (22:69, Acts 2:33-35), and the New Testament reads the ‘until’ as the time of the church, before the last enemy is destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:25-26).

The verse announces Christ's exaltation at the very moment of his humiliation. Luke's ‘from now on’ means that the cross and the throne are not two separate stages far apart but one movement, which Acts proclaims when it says God exalted Jesus to his right hand (Acts 2:33, 5:31).

Glory comes through suffering, not around it. The necessity Jesus names is not fate but God's plan written beforehand, in which the Messiah's path to his throne runs through the cross (Philippians 2:8-9, 1 Peter 1:11).
The ascension is the exaltation of the crucified one to God's presence, the entrance into glory of which verse 26 spoke.
Hupsoō makes the crucifixion itself the first step of Jesus' exaltation. In John the cross is not a defeat reversed by the resurrection but the hour of glory (12:23, 17:1).
The one who comes from heaven is above all. The verse places Jesus above every other witness, John the Baptist included, not because John spoke falsely but because he spoke as one from the earth.

In Daniel the one like a son of man receives dominion and a kingdom that will not pass away. Jesus claims that authority now, before his death, as the Son of Man who will be lifted up and glorified (3:14, 12:23).

The descent of the bread from heaven is completed by the ascent of the Son of Man. John frames the Gospel with this movement (3:13, 20:17), and verse 62 implies that the flesh given for the world will not remain in the grave to be eaten crudely but will be raised and glorified.

The cross is where the divine identity of Jesus will be made known. John does not treat the lifting up on the cross and the exaltation to glory as two separate events but as one movement, so the moment of greatest humiliation is the moment of revelation.
All things are already in the Son's hands. The authority he will exercise as the exalted Lord (Matthew 28:18) is the same authority he uses to serve.

Jesus is going to the Father, and the disciples are told to rejoice at it. The verse looks past the cross to the Son's return to the glory he had before creation, the movement Paul describes in Philippians 2:6-11.

Jesus' going to the Father is gain, not loss. The disciples will have him in a new way, through the Spirit, everywhere and at once, rather than bodily in one place, which is the sense in which the church has understood his departure to be to their advantage.

The ascension is God's verdict on the crucified. Jesus' going to the Father overturns the world's judgment and declares him righteous, which is why the apostles preached the resurrection and exaltation as God's reversal of what the rulers had done (Acts 2:23-24, 2:36).
The return to the Father completes the movement the incarnation began. Paul's hymn describes the same shape, the one in the form of God emptying himself and being highly exalted (Philippians 2:6-11).

The authority over all humanity recalls the one like a son of man in Daniel 7:14, to whom dominion over all peoples is given, and the Son of Man to whom the Father has given authority to judge (5:27). The risen Jesus claims it in Matthew 28:18.

In John the resurrection is the beginning of Jesus' return to the Father, which is his exaltation (13:1, 16:28). The present ‘I am ascending’ joins Easter to the ascension as one movement of the Son going back to the glory he had before the world began (17:5).
Jesus is exalted to the place of shared rule with God. Luke will narrate the same scene from heaven in Stephen's vision of the Son of Man standing at God's right hand (7:55-56).

Sitting at God's right hand is not rest from work but the place of rule. The enemies are still being subdued, so the church lives in the time between enthronement and final victory (1 Corinthians 15:25).

‘Lord’ in this sermon is the title of the one on whom Joel said all must call (verse 21). By applying it to the exalted Jesus, Peter places him where Israel's Scripture placed God, while still distinguishing him from the God who made him Lord.

Christ at God's right hand fulfills Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse the New Testament cites and echoes more often than any other. Paul adds that he ‘is interceding for us’, as Hebrews 7:25 also teaches: the exalted Christ is an advocate, not an accuser.
The risen Christ reigns now, seated in the place Psalm 110 promised. His reign is not postponed to the future; it is the present age, and it will go on until the last enemy is destroyed.
Christ was not only raised but enthroned at God's right hand. The resurrection is not the end of the story but the beginning of his reign.
Christ's authority is universal and permanent, spanning this age and the next. There is no name, invoked or feared, that stands above his.

Christ's enthronement at God's right hand (1:20) is not only his; believers share his seat. The New Testament picture of the saints reigning with Christ (2 Timothy 2:12, Revelation 3:21) is here described as already true in principle.

God's exaltation of Jesus is the Father's verdict on the Son's obedience. The verse does not say the Son became divine; it says the one who was in the form of God and humbled himself is now publicly given the name and rule that belong to God.

The verse describes the Son's enthronement as the moment his superiority over angels was publicly established. Hebrews holds together an eternal Sonship (verse 2) and an exaltation after suffering (2:9) without treating them as rivals.
The Son is seated in the place of highest honor and shared rule. The subjection of his enemies is still being worked out, so the exaltation is both accomplished and awaiting completion.
The crowning follows the suffering. Jesus is the first human being to receive the glory and honor Psalm 8 promised, and he received it by way of death.

The ascension is described in priestly terms: Jesus passed through the heavens as the high priest passed through the curtain. His exaltation is also his entry into the sanctuary on behalf of his people.
Jesus' entry into the heavenly sanctuary is his exaltation seen in priestly terms. The one seated at God's right hand (1:3) is also the high priest who has passed the curtain.
The exalted Christ is the priest believers need: holy in character and raised above every created height, so that nothing stands between him and God's presence.
Christ's session at God's right hand is the ‘main point’. His priesthood is exercised from the throne, which means his sacrifice is complete and his authority is universal.
Christ's entry into heaven is his ascension read as priestly entry. He is present before the Father ‘for us’, so the ascension is not his absence from his people but his representation of them.
Christ's sitting down is the sign that his sacrifice is finished. His exaltation is not only a reward but a statement about the completeness of the atonement.

The verse passes straight from birth to the throne, so that the ascension becomes the answer to the dragon's threat. Christ's exaltation to God's throne is the event that decides the war the rest of the chapter describes.
